stories.headline: Denver Water to vote on banning all lawn watering this fall amid historic drought
stories.summary:
Denver Water's Board of Water Commissioners is set to vote Wednesday on whether to prohibit its 1.5 million customers from watering grass after Sept. 30, before the typical first freeze. The proposed rule builds on existing twice-weekly outdoor watering restrictions and would represent one of the utility's most aggressive drought-response measures to date. Exceptions would apply for public parks and athletic facilities with board approval, and customers could still water trees, shrubs, flowers and vegetables by hand or non-spray irrigation.

The drought driving the proposal has been severe. Streamflow into Denver Water's reservoirs was less than a quarter of normal this year — the lowest in 110 years of recordkeeping — and reservoir levels stand at 73% full when they are normally 94% full at this time of year. This summer is also the hottest on record for metro Denver, with temperatures routinely running several degrees above average.

Denver Water had hoped to achieve a 20% reduction in water use through mandatory rules and voluntary conservation this summer but has fallen short of that target. Banning grass watering after Sept. 30 could save an estimated 5,000 acre-feet of water, enough for at least 10,000 families' annual use. The board meeting is scheduled for 9 a.m. Wednesday.

stories.headline: Denver launches citywide strangulation protocol to combat domestic violence 'hidden epidemic'
stories.summary:
Denver officials announced Tuesday a new, coordinated citywide approach to identifying and responding to domestic violence strangulation cases, which account for nearly 60% of the city's ongoing felony domestic violence cases. Thirteen city agencies — including Denver Health, Denver 911, and the police, fire and safety departments — committed to following a newly developed 39-page strangulation protocol outlining best practices for police officers, paramedics and healthcare workers.

District Attorney John Walsh called strangulation a 'hidden epidemic' at a news conference at the Rose Andom Center, noting that victims often show no visible injuries and may not report the act alongside other forms of abuse, causing first responders to miss critical intervention opportunities. Strangulation is considered a major risk factor for domestic violence homicide.

The announcement comes amid a sustained rise in domestic violence in Denver. Police reported 7,660 domestic violence incidents in 2025, up about 3% from 2024 and up 46% from 2019. The DA's office pursued 411 felony domestic violence strangulation cases in 2025 and 190 so far this year. City leaders hope consistent, cross-agency protocols will help prevent fatal outcomes.

stories.headline: Denver DSA endorses Councilwoman Shontel Lewis in challenge to Mayor Mike Johnston
stories.summary:
The Denver chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America has endorsed Councilwoman Shontel Lewis in her campaign to unseat first-term Mayor Mike Johnston in next year's city election. The chapter's roughly 2,000 members voted to support Lewis following an internal candidate forum process, DSA leaders said Tuesday. Lewis filed to run for mayor last month, forgoing a defense of her council seat representing the northeast 8th District.

Lewis joins a field that includes repeat progressive candidate Lisa Calderón and several others challenging Johnston, who was elected in 2023. The DSA also backed Lewis in her successful 2023 council campaign. 'Shontel Lewis has spent her career advancing socialist policies to help working people,' said co-chair Katie Blakey, citing Denver's budget crisis as a driving factor in the endorsement.

The endorsement carries political weight following a strong DSA showing in recent primaries. In June, DSA-backed candidate Melat Kiros defeated longtime U.S. Rep. Diana DeGette in Colorado's 1st Congressional District Democratic primary. Denver's mayoral election is scheduled for April 2027.

stories.headline: Denver Post examines what became of Trump administration's investigations into Colorado institutions
stories.summary:
A Denver Post investigation found that federal probes launched by the Trump administration against Colorado institutions have produced inconsistent and often limited follow-through, despite high-profile announcements targeting diversity programs, all-gender bathrooms and transgender athletes in K-12 schools, and conditions in state prisons. In one case, federal investigators never acted on their initial demands; in another, they sought and received thousands of documents and conducted site visits.

Colorado institutions responded in markedly different ways. Denver Public Schools publicly defied federal demands over an all-gender bathroom at East High School and was met by what DPS Superintendent Alex Marrero described as radio silence for months — until the government ultimately found a Title IX violation and gave DPS 10 days to comply or face enforcement. Jeffco Public Schools took preemptive legal action, while the University of Colorado's Colorado Springs campus quietly and quickly resolved its allegations.

Experts quoted in the story say the administration's approach is deliberate — flooding media with announcements to intimidate institutions into compliance without conducting rigorous investigations. 'In a lot of these instances, it feels like fishing,' said Beau C. Tremitiere of Protect Democracy. The story offers a comprehensive accounting of four specific federal investigations and their current status.

stories.headline: United Airlines to launch nonstop Denver-to-Paris route, expanding international service at DIA
stories.summary:
United Airlines announced Tuesday that it will add year-round nonstop service between Denver International Airport and Paris, operated on a Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner. The new route complements United's existing transatlantic service from Newark, Washington Dulles, Chicago and San Francisco, and reflects the airline's continued investment in Denver, which it calls its fastest-growing hub.

United has invested nearly $1 billion at DIA since 2021 and currently serves more than 200 destinations from Denver, including more than 20 international cities. The Paris announcement is part of a broader expansion that includes 10 new international destinations and three new routes across Europe and Asia, along with the debut of the airline's Airbus A321XLR narrowbody aircraft on select routes beginning in December.

Patrick Quayle, United's senior vice president of global network planning, said the airline is adding capacity 'at a nice measured rate where the market can absorb it' and described the Paris route as consistent with a methodical investment strategy in Denver. A start date for the Denver-Paris service was not specified in the announcement, though other new international routes begin as early as March 2027.

stories.headline: Two teenagers killed in suspected murder-suicide at Lakewood home
stories.summary:
Two teenagers were found dead from apparent gunshot wounds Monday morning at a home in the 1200 block of Benton Street in Lakewood in what police are investigating as a suspected murder-suicide. Officers responded at 9:43 a.m. after a 911 caller reported multiple people had been shot at the residence. The victims were identified as Yorbelis Del Valle Gutierrez-Arenas, 18, and a 16-year-old boy whose name was withheld because he is a juvenile.

Lakewood Police Department spokesperson John Romero said the identity of the suspected shooter had not been released because the investigation remains ongoing. No additional suspects were named and police did not provide information on the relationship between the two victims.

The Lakewood Police Department released details of the incident Tuesday in a news release. The case remains under active investigation.

stories.headline: Aurora City Council moves forward with new regulations on data centers, targeting water use and zoning
stories.summary:
The Aurora City Council approved advancing two new regulations governing data center development in the city, directing staff to return with additional proposals at a future study session. The first measure, heading to an official vote at the next regular council meeting, would ban evaporative cooling mechanisms at data centers, which city documents describe as inefficient users of water at a time when Aurora's growing population has made water supply a significant concern.

The second measure involves a zoning code change that would allow data centers in medium-industrial and business-tech zones but prohibit them in mixed-use office and institutional zones — areas that also accommodate schools and assisted living facilities. Because it involves zoning, the change must first go before a planning commission before returning to the council for a final vote later this year.

Councilmembers also debated additional regulatory options in Monday's study session, asking staff to develop proposals on setbacks, noise regulation, physical screening and size distinctions between large-scale and smaller data centers. Aurora's action reflects a broader regional push to manage the rapid proliferation of data center facilities across the Denver metro area.

stories.headline: Douglas County voters to weigh $54 million mill levy override for DougCo schools
stories.summary:
Douglas County voters will decide this fall whether to approve a $54 million mill levy override for Douglas County School District, a measure that would increase local property taxes to fund school operations. Supporters argue the funding is essential for maintaining educational programs and staffing, while opponents have raised concerns about the tax burden on property owners.

The mill levy override would represent a significant funding commitment for one of Colorado's largest suburban school districts. Colorado school districts frequently rely on voter-approved mill levy overrides to supplement state per-pupil funding, which critics say has not kept pace with the cost of running schools.

Denver7's Douglas County reporter is covering community reaction from both supporters and detractors as the measure heads toward the ballot.

stories.headline: Spa operator proposes boutique wellness complex on former Greyhound site in Denver's Curtis Park
stories.summary:
Circle Wellness, a Canadian spa operator, has proposed constructing 13 small pavilion-style buildings totaling 5,200 square feet on a nearly one-acre vacant lot at 2450 Curtis St. in Denver's Curtis Park neighborhood — the former site of a Greyhound bus maintenance facility demolished in 2023. Each structure would contain a hot and cold plunge, shower and sauna, designed to be rented by a single guest party at a time. Sessions at the company's existing locations in Vancouver and Seattle run 90 to 120 minutes and cost between $225 and $285.

Circle Wellness CEO Scott Emslie said the company is 'assessing the feasibility of a Denver location' but has not committed to moving forward. The format is described in the application as 'intentionally quiet, small-scale, and appointment-based,' suited for compact urban infill sites. Pomeroy Lodging LP, a Canadian hospitality company, is a partner in the venture.

The Curtis Park lot is still owned by FirstGroup Services, a British transportation company that acquired Greyhound in 2007 and sold it in 2021. The company did not respond to a request for comment. Adjacent parcels on the former Greyhound footprint were sold to Denver developer Corum Real Estate Group in 2022 for apartment construction.

stories.headline: Nonprofit plans new Denver Oktoberfest celebration to strengthen economic ties with Munich
stories.summary:
A Denver-based nonprofit is planning a new Oktoberfest celebration designed to deepen economic and cultural ties between Denver and Munich, Germany. The two-weekend event, scheduled for October, will feature authentic German beer, a delegation from Munich and free entry for attendees.

The event is being organized with involvement from Denver's Honorary German Consul, Chadwick Williams, according to the Denver Business Journal. Organizers say the partnership aims to go beyond the traditional festival format and cement formal economic connections between the two cities.

Details on the specific dates and venue were not disclosed in initial reporting. The celebration would add to Denver's existing Oktoberfest tradition, which has historically drawn large crowds to Civic Center Park.

stories.headline: Broncos' Vance Joseph detects opposing teams' first-down tendencies aimed at neutralizing Denver pass rush
stories.summary:
Defensive coordinator Vance Joseph said Tuesday that he has identified a clear trend in how opponents are scheming against Denver's pass rush through two preseason games: teams are relying on bootlegs, misdirection, outside runs and quick-game passes on first down to avoid falling into long-yardage situations where the Broncos' edge rushers can dominate. The Broncos led the NFL with a franchise-record 68 sacks last season and held opponents to the worst third- and fourth-down success rate in the league.

'Teams don't want to lose first down, because if they do lose first down, then our rush kind of comes alive,' Joseph said after practice. He noted that both the Atlanta Falcons and Green Bay Packers employed the strategy in their respective preseason matchups against Denver. Denver allowed a 36.76% success rate on first and second downs last season, the lowest mark in the NFL.

Joseph said the staff anticipated the adjustment after studying film over the offseason and believes the early preseason film has confirmed their expectations for how regular-season opponents will attack. Ten of Denver's 12 second-down sacks last season came in second-and-7 or longer situations, underlining why opponents are determined to stay out of obvious passing downs.

stories.headline: Broncos teammates say Bo Nix is 'playing out of his mind' heading into Year 3
stories.summary:
Denver Broncos players and coaches say quarterback Bo Nix has looked sharp through training camp and two preseason games as he enters his third NFL season, with linebacker Alex Singleton offering an emphatic endorsement: 'He's playing out of his mind.' Nix, who underwent two ankle surgeries in the offseason, has shown no apparent physical limitations in practice or in Friday's preseason game against Green Bay, shifting attention away from his recovery and toward expectations for his performance in the regular season.

Offensive coordinator Davis Webb said earlier this month that Nix is 'right on par with the other guys I've been around going into Year 3,' a comparison that has particular resonance given Webb's firsthand experience watching Josh Allen make a dramatic leap in his third season with the Buffalo Bills in 2020. Nix has led Denver to the playoffs in each of his first two seasons, though several advanced metrics have placed him in the middle tier of NFL quarterbacks.

The Broncos are betting that a combination of factors — Webb calling plays for the first time, the addition of wide receiver Jaylen Waddle, a dominant defense and Nix's continued development — will propel the team deeper into the postseason. Webb described the Year 3 jump as significant based on his personal experience and observations of other quarterbacks, calling it a more meaningful inflection point than the Year 1-to-Year 2 transition that typically draws more attention.
